messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David, a 56-year-old combat pilot, had always prided himself on his steady hands and unwavering composure, qualities essential for his demanding career. That changed irrevocably two years ago during a routine training flight when a catastrophic engine failure led to an uncontrolled descent. The deafening explosion that ripped through the cockpit was followed by a sickening lurch and a loss of all power, plunging him into a terrifying spiral. He fought the controls, enduring extreme G-forces that left him profoundly dizzy and feeling terribly ill, convinced he was moments from death. Though he miraculously ejected, surviving with severe injuries, the experience fundamentally altered his reality.

In the aftermath, David found himself trapped in a relentless internal battle. Any sudden, loud bang or explosion sound, even a car backfiring, would immediately send his body into a state of intense readiness, feeling constantly tense and poised to react to danger. He would startle to movement, his heart pounding, reacting as if he were in imminent peril, a direct consequence of the triggers now embedded in his nervous system. These triggers weren't merely external; a sudden wave of dizziness, reminiscent of the G-forces, or the onset of feeling physically unwell, would also provoke the same heightened threat response.

His perceptions of the world shifted dramatically. The accident completely shattered his core beliefs about how the world works; where he once saw order and control, he now saw chaos and unpredictability, certain that the world is a dangerous place. This profound conviction that danger lurked everywhere, coupled with his hypervigilance – constantly being superalert and on guard – made him exquisitely sensitive to any potential trigger, amplifying their impact. He also began to experience a deep emotional numbness, feeling dead inside, a stark contrast to his once vibrant personality, and this feeling reinforced his belief that the world was too dangerous for genuine joy or connection.

To cope with the constant sense of threat and his shattered worldview, David began implementing a range of maladaptive strategies. He started to restrict his eating, meticulously controlling his food intake in an attempt to regain some semblance of control over his body when his mind felt utterly out of control. This struggle for internal mastery, however, did little to quell the underlying fear. What began as a subtle shift grew into a pervasive pattern: his belief that the world is a dangerous place led him to stop enjoying many pleasant activities he once cherished, retreating from social engagements and hobbies, further deepening his emotional numbness. He also found himself increasingly avoiding any medical cues – hospitals, ambulances, even routine physical examinations – because the thought of doctors or medical settings would make him feel physically unwell, which in turn would trigger his body to feel on alert, perpetuating the cycle of anxiety.

This avoidance had insidious consequences for David, both personally and professionally. His tendency to avoid medical cues meant he often dismissed genuine physical discomfort, fearing that addressing it would only exacerbate his feeling of being unwell and put his body on alert. This made him more vulnerable to the very sensations that acted as triggers. Moreover, the constant threat response, his body on alert and startling to movement, was mentally exhausting and led him to restrict his eating and give up enjoyment. His wife, Maria, noticed his increasing withdrawal and the profound emotional numbness that settled over him. When he began to avoid his annual flight physicals, citing vague excuses, his commanding officer put him on administrative leave, a devastating blow to a man whose identity was so intertwined with flying.

The self-reinforcing loops tightened. His maladaptive strategies, such as stopping enjoyment and avoiding medical cues, did nothing to challenge his negative appraisals; in fact, they only reinforced his belief that the world is a dangerous place and cemented his emotional numbness. This made him even more hypervigilant, causing him to perceive even more ordinary stimuli as triggers, thus amplifying his threat response. Now, even the feeling of being physically unwell, a minor symptom, became a potent trigger, leading him to further restrict his eating in a desperate attempt to feel in control. This spiraling cycle of fear, avoidance, and emotional deadness finally brought David to seek help, desperate to reclaim some part of the life he had lost, yet deeply afraid that the world truly was as dangerous as it felt, and that he was irrevocably broken.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not explicitly state how current triggers directly lead to or reinforce negative appraisals.
